summary: Gyatsho Tshering (1936–2009) was a Tibetologist who studied at the University of Calcutta. He founded the Library of Tibetan Works and Archives, serving as its Acting Director in 1972 and Director from 1974 to 1998.

Gyoei Fukuda (1867–1954), a Buddhist studies scholar educated at Tendai Daigakurin, served as president of Taisho University around 1926–1943. He was also a part-time professor at the University of Tokyo in 1928 and lectured at Toyo University.

Gyoei Takahashi (b. 1941) is a Buddhist studies scholar. Affiliated with Rissho University as an assistant professor (attested 2003–2004) and professor (attested 2026), he was also a member of the Institute for the Comprehensive Study of the Lotus Sutra (attested 2004).

Gyoko Iotani (b. 1949), a Buddhist studies scholar, studied at Rissho University (~1968–1978) and later served there as assistant professor (~1980–1990), professor (~1990–2020), and professor emeritus (~2020). He is also attested at Minobusan University (2026).

Gyokusen Hosaka (1887–1964) was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at Komazawa University from around 1906 to 1911. He later served as president of Komazawa Junior College from around 1950 to 1962.
Gyomay Kubose (1905–2000) was a scholar of Buddhist and religious studies. He studied at Otani University and under Haya Akegarasu from around 1928 to 1934.
Gyoon Iotani is a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at Waseda University (attested 2015). By 2026, he is attested as assistant director at Minobusan University.
Gyosho Takahashi (b. 1949) is a Buddhist studies scholar. He was a professor at Minobusan Junior College (attested 1992) and Minobusan University (attested 1996).

Gyoshu Chojo is a Buddhist studies scholar who served as a professor at Minobusan Junior College (attested 1996) and as a professor in the Faculty of Buddhist Studies at Minobusan University (attested 2001).

Gyula Benigny (1890–1966) was an Indologist and linguist who earned his Ph.D. at Eötvös Loránd University (~1908–1912). He taught at Debrecen Reformed Theological University and served as docent (1917) and extraordinary professor (1932–1949) at the University of Debrecen.
Gyula Ortutay (1910–1978) studied at the University of Szeged (1928–1934) and held a post at Nyugat.
Gyula Wojtilla (b. 1945) is an Indologist who studied under János Harmatta (~1963–1968), at Eötvös Loránd University (1964–1969), and at Banaras Hindu University (~1972–1974).

Gyurme Dorje (1950–2020) was a Tibetologist and Buddhist studies scholar educated at the University of Edinburgh and SOAS. He held fellowships at SOAS/University of London (1991–1996) and worked as a translator for the Tsadra Foundation (2007–2020).
Gyurme Pema Tekchok studied under Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche and Jamgon Ju Mipham Gyatso.

György Hazai (1932–2016) was a scholar of linguistics and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Eötvös Loránd University (~1949–1954) and held a post at the Institut für Orientforschung from around 1963 to 1982.

György Kara (1935–2022) was a linguistics and Central Asian studies scholar educated at Eötvös Loránd University, the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, and Saint Petersburg State University. He held posts at Eötvös Loránd University, the Hungarian Academy, and Indiana University Bloomington (1993–2022).

Gyōin Hashimoto (1897–1978) was a scholar of Buddhist studies and philosophy who studied under Join Saeki and at the University of Tokyo (~1921–1925). He served as head of Yakushiji (1939–1967) and head of the Hosso School (1940).

Gábor Kovács is a scholar of Buddhist studies and philosophy. He earned an MA at Dharma Gate Buddhist College (2005–2010) and a PhD at Corvinus University of Budapest (2010–2017), where he became an associate professor in 2018.
Gé Mang Khenchen Yönten Gyatso studied under Patrul Rinpoche and Jamgon Ju Mipham Gyatso, and taught Shechen Gyaltsab.

Gérard Barrigue de Fontainieu (1863–1927) was an Indologist who earned his diploma from the Institut national des langues et civilisations orientales by 1891. He held a pensionnaire post at the École française d'Extrême-Orient from 1901 to 1902.
